==Background==

On February 18, 2014, the Mozambican government approved a coal-fired project with a capacity of 600 MW. The project would have been run by ACWA Power Moatize Termoelectrica SA, a consortium whose main shareholders are ACWA Power of Saudi Arabia, Vale of Brazil, and Mitsui of Japan. The power station was to be located at the mouth of the open cast Moatize coal mine, operated by Vale. The higher grade coal (particularly coking coal) mined by Vale was to be exported, while the lower grade coal was to be burnt in the power station.<ref name=cm>[http://www.clubofmozambique.com/solutions1/sectionnews.php?secao=mining&id=31548&tipo=one "Moatize coal-fired station gets the go-ahead,"] Club of Mozambique, February 20, 2014</ref>

Construction of the power station was expected to take three years. The project was going to be built in two phases. The first phase was to involve the construction of a 300 MW plant for US$1 billion.<ref>[http://www.macauhub.com.mo/en/2015/03/02/mozambiques-energy-sector-sees-investments-of-us3-2-billion-in-2014/ "Mozambique’s energy sector sees investments of US$3.2 billion in 2014,"] Macau Hub, March 2, 2015</ref> The plant would have been a pulverized fuel, sub-critical power station. About 250 MW of the total capacity of 300 MW would feed the [[Moatize mine]], with the remaining 50 MW supplied to the national grid.<ref name=esi>[http://www.esi-africa.com/mozambique-approves-600-mw-coal-fired-power-station/ "Mozambique approves 600 MW coal fired power station,"] ESI Africa, March 17, 2014</ref>

The sponsors selected international contractor GS Engineering & Construction from Korea for the engineering, procurement and construction of the project, and ACWA Power’s wholly owned subsidiary NOMAC was going to be responsible for the operation and maintenance of the plant.<ref name=esi>[http://www.esi-africa.com/mozambique-approves-600-mw-coal-fired-power-station/ "Mozambique approves 600 MW coal fired power station,"] ESI Africa, March 17, 2014</ref>

According to ACWA Power (May 2016), the power station was planned to be 270 MW. ACWA said it had one PPA with Vale MZ for 220 MW, and another with Electricidad de Mozambique for 50 MW. The project was seeking half a billion dollars in financing from multilateral lenders and export credit agencies. Commercial operation was planned for Q1 2018.<ref>[http://acwapower.com/project/moatize-ipp/ "Projects,"] ACWA Power, accessed May 2016</ref>

As of 2021, the project was removed from the ACWA website and there were no known developments in securing financing. The project appeared to be shelved or cancelled.

==Ownership and financing==

ACWA held 56.5% of the power station project, with smaller shareholdings by Mitsui of Japan and Vale, while Mozambican company Whatana Investment Group has 8% and Electricidad de Mozambique owns 5%. The estimated cost was US$1 billion. ACWA was trying to raise funding from various export credit agencies and multilateral and development financing agencies. The amount required from these sources exceeded US$500 million according to ACWA.<ref>[http://www.engineeringnews.co.za/article/some-progress-visible-on-mozambican-coal-miners-power-station-projects-2016-03-25/rep_id:4136 "Mozambique coal miners’ power station projects making ‘visible progress’"] Engineering News, March 25, 2016</ref>

According to a March 2016 report, Paddy Padmanathan, CEO of ACWA Power, described finding financing for the plant as "turning out to be quite a challenge." Padmanathan said that there had been "a few different configurations on the financing structure." The report said that Korean engineering firm GS would build the plant, meaning that Korean export promotion bank KEXIM was likely to be one of the financiers. Another possible lender was the African Development Bank.<ref>Max Ndianaefo, [http://www.cp-africa.com/2016/03/24/mozambique-coal-fired-power-project-seek-lenders/ "Mozambique: Coal-Fired Power project seek lenders,"] CPAFRICA, March 24, 2016</ref>

==Coal mine==

The plant would be constructed in Tete province, where Vale has developed and is operating the biggest coal mine in the world, the [[Moatize mine]].<ref name=kc>Keith Campbell, [http://www.miningweekly.com/print-version/mozambique-set-to-get-hydrocarbons-billions-and-vale-unveils-power-station-plan-2012-09-28 "Mozambique set to get hydrocarbons billions, Vale unveils power station plan,"] Mining Weekly, September 28, 2012</ref>

Brazilian mining company Vale has been present in Mozambique since 2004 with the Moatize coal mine. The company mined 3.77 million megatonnes of metallurgical and thermal coal in its first full year of operations in 2012. Moatize phase II is scheduled for 2015, and Vale said it would increase production at the mine to 22 million megatonnes annually, including five million megatonnes of thermal coal. Vale is also constructing the Nacala Corridor to connect Moatize to the [[Nacala port]], and restoring Sena Railway to connect Moatize to the [[Beira port]].<ref>[http://macigindaba.com/2014/09/09/mozambique-a-waking-coal-giant/ "Mozambique: a Waking Coal Giant,"] MACIG, September 9, 2014</ref>

In January 2014 Mitsui said it had agreed to pay nearly US$450 million for a 15 per cent stake in the Brazilian group’s Moatize mine, and invest a further US$188 million to fund the mine's expansion. Mitsui also agreed to pay US$313 million for a 50 per cent stake in Vale’s subsidiary that has been promoting the multibillion dollar [[Nacala port]] and rail project.<ref>[http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/887f03b2-7fb4-11e4-b4f5-00144feabdc0.html#axzz3RT10D0yZ "Mitsui invests $1bn in Vale’s Mozambique coal projects,"] ft, December 9, 2014</ref>

==Background==

Ambatovy Nickel power station is a three-unit coal-fired power plant with a total capacity of 120 MW, powering the operations of the Ambatovy nickel mine. The plant was completed in 2011, and was originally owned by a joint venture of Sherritt International, Sumitomo, Korea Resources Corp. (KORES), and SNC-Lavalin. The mine's commercial operation was achieved in 2014. The mined ore is transferred to an on-site ore preparation plant for separating laterite from waste and mixing water to it to produce ore slurry. The ore slurry is fed through a pipeline system that links the mine to the processing plant located 220km away and 11km south of the Port of Toamasina.<ref>[https://ambatovy.com/ang/who-we-are/history/ "History of the project,"] Ambatovy, accessed May 27, 2021</ref><ref>[https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/projects/ambatovy-nickel-cobalt-project/ "Ambatovy Nickel-Cobalt Project,"] NS Energy, accessed May 27, 2021</ref>

In 2015, partner SNC-Lavalin sold its participation in Ambatovy’s capital to Sumitomo Corporation.<ref>[https://www.snclavalin.com/en/media/press-releases/2015/30-09-2015 "SNC-Lavalin exercises its option to sell its interest in Madagascar’s Ambatovy Nickel Project,"] SNC-Lavalin, September 30, 2015</ref> Sherritt reduced its share in Ambatovy’s capital from 40% to 12% in 2017, and then to nothing in 2020.<ref name=":0">[https://www.spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/metals/032621-madagascars-ambatovy-restarts-nickel-production#:~:text=London%20%E2%80%94%20Madagascan%20nickel%20and%20cobalt,nickel%20briquettes%20on%20March%2023 "Madagascar's Ambatovy restarts nickel production,"] S&P Global, March 26, 2021</ref>

Ambatovy halted nickel production for a year due to national COVID-19 lockdown restrictions.<ref name=":0">[https://www.spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/metals/032621-madagascars-ambatovy-restarts-nickel-production#:~:text=London%20%E2%80%94%20Madagascan%20nickel%20and%20cobalt,nickel%20briquettes%20on%20March%2023 "Madagascar's Ambatovy restarts nickel production,"] S&P Global, March 26, 2021</ref>

In August 2020, the South Korean government announced plans to sell its stakes in 'loss-making' mines', including the Ambatovy plant. As of April 2022, however, the new President Yoon Suk-yeol has chosen to rescind this motion and instead invite private-sector companies to lead international energy projects in the government's stead.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kedglobal.com/energy/newsView/ked202204070010|title=S.Korea to scrap plans to sell Ambatovy mine stake|last=Global|first=K. E. D.|website=KED Global|language=en|access-date=2022-05-25}}</ref> 

A 2022 journal article published in ''Nature Sustainability'' claims that the Ambatovy Nickel power station will be the first mine in the world to fully offset deforestation and biodiversity losses caused by its processes.<ref>Devenish, K., Desbureaux, S., Willcock, S. ''et al.'' On track to achieve no net loss of forest at Madagascar’s biggest mine. ''Nat Sustain'' (2022). <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-022-00850-7</nowiki></ref> This "controversial accolade" involves many caveats and lacks concrete evaluation. Representatives from Ambatovy are in support of the study and say that they are committed to acting responsibly, despite claims of odor and water pollution connected to the plant.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/mar/09/ambatovy-the-madagascan-mine-that-might-prove-carbon-offsetting-works-aoe|title=Is a Madagascan mine the first to offset its destruction of rainforest?|date=2022-03-09|website=the Guardian|language=en|access-date=2022-05-25}}</ref>

In November 2024, it was reported that operations at the Ambatovy nickel and cobalt plant had been suspended for a month due to a pipeline rupture before gradually resuming. It was also noted that the facility had been unable to meet its production targets, resulting in a significant loss in value of nearly $600 million. In light of these challenges, it was reported that Sumitomo was considering selling its controlling stake in the project to another company.<ref>[https://www.ecofinagency.com/mining/0411-46103-japans-sumitomo-plans-to-sell-madagascars-largest-nickel-mine "Japan's Sumitomo Plans to Sell Madagascar's Largest Nickel Mine,"] EcoFin Agency, November 4, 2024</ref> As of November 2025, no sale or transfer of ownership had been reported.

It was confirmed in October 2025 that production at the plant had not been affected by recent political instability, and that scheduled maintenance shutdowns in November were proceeding as planned.<ref>[https://discoveryalert.com.au/ambatovy-nickel-project-madagascar-2025-production-2025/ "Ambatovy Nickel Project Weathers Madagascar’s Political Upheaval,"] Discovery Alert, October 31, 2025</ref>

As of February 2026, the Ambatovy nickel and cobalt plant had suspended operations due to damage caused by Tropical Cyclone Gezani.<ref>[https://www.miningweekly.com/article/sumitomos-madagascar-project-ambatovy-remains-shut-due-to-cyclone-damage-2026-02-18 “Sumitomo's Madagascar project Ambatovy remains shut due to cyclone damage,”] Mining Weekly, February 18, 2026</ref>

==Background==

In February 2016 Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Ernst & Young ShinNihon LLC, and Japan External Trade Organization released a study of a 3 x 150 MW coal plant sponsored by Asahi Glass at Ayer near Cilegon in Banten province. According to the report, plants of 600 MW in size and using [[ultrasupercritical]] combustion were initially studied, modeled after the [[Hirono power station]]
in Japan; however, such plants would require bituminous coal, which in Indonesia is reserved for export. For domestically available subbituminous coal, the study observed that a unit size of 1,000 MW or larger would be necessary. For smaller units, ultra-supercritical combustion was considered to be impractical with Indonesian subbitumious coal due to the expensive materials that would be necessary to prevent corrosion. For that reason, the study covered not only ultra-supercritical but also supercritical, subcritical, and circulating fluidized bed combustion.<ref>[http://www.meti.go.jp/meti_lib/report/2015fy/000467.pdf Study on Coal-Fired Power Plant in Anyer, The Republic of Indonesia,"] Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Erst & Young ShinNihon LLC, and Japan External Trade Organization, February 2015</ref>

In April 2015 Asahi Glass of Japan said it plans to build a 250 MW coal-fired power plant in Indonesia, at the site of the company's Asahimas Chemical factory to generate its own electricity for producing chemical products. The company plans to spend a total of US$400 million on the project. The plant would use locally produced coal, as well as some biomass fuel. It is scheduled to go online in 2017, according to the sources.<ref>[http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Companies/Asahi-Glass-plans-coal-plant-to-power-production "Asahi Glass plans coal plant to power production,"] Nikkei, Apr 8, 2015</ref>

In April 2016 Kawasaki Heavy Industries said it had received an order from Taiwanese company Formosa Heavy Industries Corp. (FHI) for two 150 MW class steam turbine power generation facilities, to install at an Asahi Glass factory in Indonesia.<ref>[https://global.kawasaki.com/en/corp/newsroom/news/detail/?f=20160425_9174 "Kawasaki to Provide Two 150 MW Steam Turbine Power Facilities to Factory in Indonesia,"] Kawasaki, Apr. 25, 2016</ref> It is planned for 2018.<ref>[http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2016/02/13/asahimas-chemical-triple-exports-year.html "Asahimas Chemical to triple exports this year,"] The Jakarta Post, February 13, 2016</ref>

Construction of the plant began in Q4 of 2016.<ref>[https://www.reportbuyer.com/product/5218059/agc-cilegon-coal-fired-power-plant-300-mw-banten-project-profile.html AGC – Cilegon Coal-Fired Power Plant 300 MW – Banten - Project Profile], Timetric, February 2018</ref> In September 2018 Asahimas' parent company Asahi Glass stated that the Banten chemical factory expansion would begin operations in Q2 2021.<ref name=acg>[https://www.agc.com/en/news/detail/1197705_2814.html AGC to Increase its PVC Production Capacity in Indonesia], AGC, Sep. 5, 2018</ref>

The Asahi Glass Company (AGC) 2020 Integrated Report and Financial Results report indicated that the power station at the Asahimas Chemical plant began operating in the second quarter of 2019.<ref>[https://www.agc.com/en/company/agc_report/pdf/agc_report_en_2020.pdf "AGC Integrated Report 2020, For the Year Ended December 31, 2019,"] AGC, May 2020</ref><ref>[https://www.agc.com/en/ir/library/briefing/pdf/2021_0205e_1.pdf "Financial Results for FY2020,"] AGC, February 5, 2021</ref> As of July 2023, [https://www.planet.com/stories/6-02deg-s-105-94deg-e-bdzbgUj4R satellite imagery from Planet] also indicated that coal shipments were arriving at the power station's jetty.

In their 2022 Integrated Report, published in July 2023, AGC stated that GHG emissions from in-house power generation facilities would be addressed on the "medium term". Solar power and the use of biofuels were both mentioned.<ref>[https://www.agc.com/en/company/agc_report/pdf/agc_report_en_2023.pdf "AGC Integrated Report 2023,"] AGC, July 3, 2023</ref> The Integrated Report published in May 2024 included the same language.<ref>[https://www.agc.com/en/company/agc_report/pdf/agc_report_en_2024.pdf "AGC Integrated Report 2024,"] AGC, May 2024</ref>

==Background==

The plant started operation in July 2016 after a 30-month construction period.<ref name='ref_M'>{{cite web |url=https://peakers.com/avon.html |title=peakers.com/avon.html |date= |access-date= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210907232754/https://peakers.com/avon.html |archive-date=September 7, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> It was built with the intention to be converted to natural gas and combined cycle technology.<ref name='ref_J'>{{cite web |url=https://hulisani.co.za/project/avon-and-dedisa-peaking-power |title=Avon and Dedisa Peaking Power Investment - Hulisani Investment Opportunity - SA |date=September 1, 2019 |access-date=January 29, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210907231949/https://hulisani.co.za/project/avon-and-dedisa-peaking-power |archive-date=September 7, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>https://www.powermag.com/press-releases/avon-peaking-power-south-africas-largest-ipp-reaches-commercial-operation-adding-670-mw-to-the-national-grid/</ref>

Together with [[Dedisa power station|Dedisa Power Station]], with a combined capacity of 1005 MW,  the privately owned power plants supply power to Eskom under with 15-year Power Purchase Agreements (“PPA).”<ref name='ref_J'>{{cite web |url=https://hulisani.co.za/project/avon-and-dedisa-peaking-power |title=Avon and Dedisa Peaking Power Investment - Hulisani Investment Opportunity - SA |date=September 1, 2019 |access-date=January 29, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210907231949/https://hulisani.co.za/project/avon-and-dedisa-peaking-power |archive-date=September 7, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Death and disease attributable to fine particle pollution from Birchwood Power Facility===

In 2010, Abt Associates issued a study commissioned by the Clean Air Task Force, a nonprofit research and advocacy organization, quantifying the deaths and other health effects attributable to [[Particulates and coal|fine particle pollution]] from coal-fired power plants.<ref>[http://www.catf.us/resources/publications/files/The_Toll_from_Coal.pdf "The Toll from Coal: An Updated Assessment of Death and Disease from America's Dirtiest Energy Source,"] Clean Air Task Force, September 2010.</ref> Fine particle pollution consists of a complex mixture of [[soot]], [[Heavy metals and coal|heavy metals]], [[Sulfur dioxide and coal|sulfur dioxide]], and [[Nitrogen oxide|nitrogen oxides]]. Among these particles, the most dangerous are those less than 2.5 microns in diameter, which are so tiny that they can evade the lung's natural defenses, enter the bloodstream, and be transported to vital organs. Impacts are especially severe among the elderly, children, and those with respiratory disease. The study found that over 13,000 deaths and tens of thousands of cases of chronic bronchitis, acute bronchitis, asthma, congestive heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, dysrhythmia, ischemic heart disease, chronic lung disease, and pneumonia each year are attributable to fine particle pollution from U.S. coal plant emissions. These deaths and illnesses are major examples of coal's [[External costs of coal|external costs]], i.e. uncompensated harms inflicted upon the public at large. [[Coal plants near residential areas|Low-income and minority populations]] are disproportionately impacted as well, due to the tendency of companies to avoid locating power plants upwind of affluent communities. To monetize the health impact of fine particle pollution from each coal plant, Abt assigned a value of $7,300,000 to each 2010 mortality, based on a range of government and private studies. Valuations of illnesses ranged from $52 for an asthma episode to $440,000 for a case of chronic bronchitis.<ref>[http://www.catf.us/resources/publications/files/Abt-Technical_Support_Document_for_the_Powerplant_Impact_Estimator_Software_Tool.pdf "Technical Support Document for the Powerplant Impact Estimator Software Tool,"] Prepared for the Clean Air Task Force by Abt Associates, July 2010</ref>

==Background==

Bluewaters power station is a 2 x 233-megawatt (MW) coal plant located 4.5 kilometres north east of Collie, Western Australia.<ref>[http://www.bluewatersps.com.au/bluewaterspowerstation.html "Bluewaters Power Station"], BlueWaters Power, BlueWaters Power website, accessed June 2014.</ref> 

[[Griffin Energy]]'s proposals for two subcritical coal-fired power station were approved by the Western Australian government in 2004 and 2005.<ref>Collie Coal, [http://www.colliecoal.com/images/collie-6--dooqu.pdf "Bluewaters decision helps secure State's energy needs"], Media Release, May 30, 2005.</ref><ref>Griffin Energy, [http://www.griffinenergy.com.au/default.aspx?MenuID=54 "Our History"], Griffin Energy website, accessed August 2008.</ref> In December 2005 the company announced that Mitsui would begin construction of the $400 million Unit 1 in early 2006 with a completion date set for 2008.<ref>[http://www.abc.net.au/news/newsitems/200512/s1533150.htm "WA set for new $400m power station"], ''ABC News'', December 17, 2005.</ref> The station was planned on the basis of using coal from Griffin’s new [[Ewington I mine]]<ref>Collie Coal, [http://www.colliecoal.com/power_generation/future_generation.phtml "Future Generation"], Collie Coal website, accessed 2008.</ref> 

The plant was initially scheduled to be commissioned in late 2008.<ref>Office of Energy, Government of Western Australia, [http://www.energy.wa.gov.au/2/3190/64/wholesale_elect.pm "Wholesale Electricity Market"], Office of Energy website, accessed August 2008.</ref> Construction of Unit 2 began in 2007 with the commissioning date pushed back to 2009.<ref>Office of Energy, Government of Western Australia, [http://www.energy.wa.gov.au/2/3190/64/wholesale_elect.pm "Wholesale Electricity Market"], Office of Energy website, accessed August 2008.</ref> Both units were commissioned in 2009.

The administrators of the Griffin Group, KordaMentha report that 93% of the power from the plant is sold "under 3 complex PPAs [Power Purchase Agreements] (and the remainder sold on market)."<ref>KordaMentha, [http://www.kordamentha.com/our-engagements/griffin-energy-group "Griffin Energy Group - Griffin Power"], KordaMetha website, accessed June 2014.</ref>

In December 2025, the Western Australian Economic Regulation Authority (ERA) fined the owners of Bluewaters power station A$5 million (US$3.3 million) for breaching the rules of the wholesale electricity market between October 2023 and June 2024. The ERA said that an investigation concluded that Bluewaters “priced its electricity at higher prices than were efficient and permitted” under market rules and estimated the company’s bidding behavior inflated market costs by about A$30 million (US$19.9 million). Bluewaters had reportedly applied to the Electricity Review Board to review the ERA decision and overturn the fine. A spokesperson for Bluewaters said the alleged breaches occurred when the utility faced coal and water shortages and was managing its generation to cater for peak demand.<ref>[https://reneweconomy.com.au/coal-generator-hit-with-heavy-fines-by-regulator-for-bidding-behaviour-and-inflating-prices/amp/ “Coal generator hit with heavy fines by regulator for bidding behaviour and inflating prices,”] Renew Economy, December 8, 2025</ref><ref>[https://www.watoday.com.au/national/western-australia/wa-s-biggest-coal-fired-power-station-to-fight-fines-for-overcharging-customers-20251208-p5nlvh.html “WA’s biggest coal-fired power station to fight fines for overcharging customers,”] WA Today, December 8, 2025</ref>

==Ownership upheavals and financial challenges==

The plant was initially built by [[Griffin Energy]]. However, following the financial collapse of the Griffin Group in January 2010 after failing to meet a payment on its $700 million of debts,<ref>[http://www.smh.com.au/business/debtladen-griffin-coal-put-into-administration-20100104-lo54.html "Debt-laden Griffin Coal put into administration"], ''Sydney Morning Herald'', January 4, 2010.</ref><ref>Colin Kruger, [http://www.smh.com.au/business/cash-crunch-rising-costs-pushed-griffin-coal-over-the-edge-20100920-15jq3.html "Cash crunch, rising costs pushed Griffin Coal over the edge"], ''Sydney Morning Herald'', September 21, 2010.</ref> the administrators sold off the power generation assets of Griffin Energy.

In January 2011 it was announced that Kansai Electric Power (KEPCO) and Sumitomo Corporation had agreed to buy the power station for approximately $1.1 billion and that the deal was expected to be finalised within two months.<ref>Andrew Burrell, [http://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/mining-energy/japanese-in-12bn-griffin-power-buy/story-e6frg9df-1226036238366?nk=eced999d8681d9d04d36ed0e55f94ebd "Japanese energy giants in $1.1bn Griffin power buy"], ''The Australian'', April 09, 2011.</ref> 

The deal was delayed by complex negotiations with [[Lanco]], which insisted on renegotiating the coal supply contracts for the power station which they argued -- after buying the mines -- that the contracted coal price was too low. Renegotiating the coal price required the administrators to renegotiate the power purchase agreements before Kansai Electric Power and Sumitomo Corporation would agree to complete the deal. By January 2012 the administrators were estimating the sale could be completed by March.<ref>Stephen Bell, [http://www.theaustralian.com.au/archive/business/sale-of-griffins-bluewater-power-stations-finalised-by-late-march/story-e6frg9e6-1226248443932 "Sale of Griffin's Bluewater power stations finalised by late March"], ''The Australian'', January 19, 2012.</ref>

However, the sale wasn't completed until mid-February 2013. Sumitomo announced that the consortium formed between it and Kansai Electric Power would "jointly manage the acquired electricity business". Sumitomo announced that its share of the project would be managed through its Sydney-headquartered wholly owned subsidiary Summit Southern Cross Power Holdings Pty Ltd. Sumitomo, which had bought a stake in the 320 MW Kwinana gas fired plant in 2009, signalled that "aims to further expand its power project business in the Australian market."<ref>Sumitomo Corporation, [http://www.sumitomocorp.com.au/110.html "Participating in Power Business in Australia"], Sumitomo Corporation website, accessed June 2014.</ref>

===Debt problems in 2020===

In July 2020, ''The Australian'' reported that an August 2020 deadline for the Bluewaters Power Station to pay back A$400m of debt would prove challenging for Sumitomo Corporation due to the fact that many international commercial banks are no longer prepared to provide finance for the thermal coal sector. It could therefore fall on the power station owners to provide their own capital to service the debt.<ref>[https://ieefa.org/debt-woes-threaten-australias-newest-coal-fired-power-plant/ "Debt deadline nearing for Bluewaters owner"], The Australian, accessed Jul. 2020 via IEEFA website</ref>

In November 2020, Sumitomo reported a US$241 million loss at the Bluewaters coal power plant as it posted record losses overall for the first half of its financial year.<ref>[https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/banking-finance/sumitomo-posts-record-h1-loss-amid-covid-crisis "Sumitomo posts record H1 loss amid Covid crisis"], The Business Times, Nov. 6, 2020</ref> In December 2020 Sumitomo wrote off its $250 million investment in the plant, evaluating the plant as worthless given Australia's turn towards other forms of energy.<ref>Daniel Mercer, [https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-12-17/bluewaters-coal-fired-power-station-written-off-books/12990532 Bluewaters coal-fired power station written off as worthless as renewables rise], ABC News, Dec. 17, 2020</ref>

In March 2021, ''The Australian Financial Review'' reported that due to climate change concerns the Australian investment management company IFM Investors had declined to get involved with a potential refinancing deal for Bluewaters. While IFM did not refer directly to Bluewaters, ''AFR'' reporting strongly suggested that the investment company's climate report had alluded to its rejection of an offered refinancing package from Bluewaters. According to IFM's climate report, "Whilst we do not typically exclude companies, IFM has declined to participate in several debt offerings principally due to a lack of alignment with our Responsible Investment Charter and ESG Policy, or due to ownership, governance or other ESG issues of the borrower (or parent of the borrower) ... For example, refinance for a power station was rejected due to concerns relating to the use of coal as the main fuel, as well as the plant's revenue reliance on a particular company that we believe lacked appropriate governance structures."<ref> Michael Roddan, [https://www.afr.com/companies/financial-services/ifm-spurned-wa-power-plant-over-coal-concerns-20210305-p578aj "IFM spurned WA power plant over coal concerns"], The Australian Financial Review, Mar. 8, 2021</ref>
In August 2022, Sumitomo initiated legal action in an attempt to take over ownership of the Griffin coal mine, because the company had failed to provide reliable coal supplies and had directly impacted the operation of the Bluewaters plant. At this point, Griffin reportedly had US$671 million in debts.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-08-31/power-plant-seeks-control-of-indian-owned-wa-coal-mine/101391152?utm_source=CoalWire&utm_campaign=00509c81c2-EMAIL_CAMPAIGN_2022_09_07_02_00&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_6826541fba-00509c81c2-208475682 "WA's biggest private power station moves to take over loss-making, Indian-owned coal mine"], ABC News, August 31, 2022.</ref> 

===Griffin Coal debts and subsidies===
In October 2022, a liquidator's audit found that Griffin Coal owed $1.41 billion to secured creditors and another $33 million to local suppliers.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-10-04/failed-griffin-coal-mine-owes-close-to-1-5-billion/101500338 "Failed Griffin Coal mine owes close to $1.5 billion to creditors as WA electricity grid woes loom"], ABC News, October 4, 2022.</ref>

In February 2023, the Western Australian Government offered Griffin Coal A$19.5 million ($13.61 million USD) to continue supplying coal to Bluewaters power station.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-02-14/wa-government-griffin-coal-bail-out/101973286 "WA government offers $19.5 million to keep struggling Griffin Coal mine operational"], ABC News, February 14, 2023.</ref>

In November 2023, the Western Australian government extended their financial support for Griffin Coal, pledging to provide A$220 million (US$144 million) to keep the Griffin coal mine operating until 2026.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-12-01/griffin-coal-mine-set-to-have-wa-government-lifeline-extended/103175824 "Foreign-owned Griffin Coal mine receives another huge WA taxpayer-funded lifeline,"] ABC News, November 30, 2023</ref>

By July 2025, Griffin Coal’s debt had reached $2.4 billion. The Western Australian state budget for 2025 reportedly set aside another $49 million for Griffin Coal to keep operating and supplying coal to Bluewaters. With this latest provision for the company, the WA government’s total support for Griffin Coal would total $308 million.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-07-07/griffin-coal-mine-debt-bluewaters-power/105492506 “Fears for WA's energy grid as Griffin Coal slides almost $1 billion further into debt,”] ABC News, July 6, 2025</ref>

In January 2026, the Western Australian government announced a five-year extension of the subsidy to keep Griffin Coal’s [[Ewington Coal Mine]] open and supplying coal to Bluewaters. The extension was set to run until 2031. The government reportedly said that detailed costs would be disclosed to state parliament “later in the year”, but that the subsidy was expected to be “significantly” reduced.<ref>[https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/western-australia-extends-coal-mine-subsidy-citing-energy-security-2026-01-21/ “Western Australia extends coal mine subsidy, citing energy security,”] Reuters, January 20, 2026</ref>

==Coal retirement==

In February 2023, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) estimated that Bluewaters power station, the youngest coal-fired project in Australia, would retire by 2029.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-02-05/bluewaters-coal-fired-power-station-to-close-by-2029/101927824?utm_campaign=The%20Canopy&utm_medium=email&_hsmi=244693250&_hsenc=p2ANqtz--_BoSNjQqOLn4T16T2XUSa14yXK3MIMUIAF9PrMcQuXbNNQ-P9tPQrj1ZuDNZz1WugcUW1KBFmW4Iowk4q8HgO_YoGUA&utm_content=244693250&utm_source=hs_email "System operator predicts Bluewaters, Australia's newest coal-fired power plant will close by 2029"], ABC News, February 4, 2023.</ref> They also modeled an expedited scenario where the power station could be shuttered by as soon as mid-2023.<ref>[https://www.aemo.com.au/-/media/files/gas/national_planning_and_forecasting/wa_gsoo/2022/2022-wa-gas-statement-of-opportunities.pdf?la=en "2022 Western Australia Gas Statement of Opportunities"], AEMO, December 2022.</ref>

===2023: Waning profitability and potentially expedited retirement===
Reporting in August 2023 stated that the Bluewaters plant was facing financial issues and could be shut down as early as 2025, though it would "likely" close near the end of the decade.<ref>[https://reneweconomy.com.au/race-to-renewables-wa-delays-closure-of-coal-unit-will-nsw-follow-suit-at-eraring/ Race to renewables: WA delays closure of coal unit, will NSW follow suit at Eraring?,] Renew Economy, August 18, 2023</ref> September reporting further noted that the power station had been running well below its regular capacity due to a shortage of available coal from its supplier, Griffin Coal.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-09-24/indian-owned-coal-mine-time-bomb-as-state-braces-for-shock/102828318 Foreign-owned Griffin coal mine a 'time bomb' as WA energy consumers brace for the fallout,] ABC News Australia, September 23, 2023</ref> In the AEMO's 2023 Wholesale Electricity Market report (published August 2023), it was estimated that the Bluewater units would close in October 2030 in the expected scenario, or in October 2025 according to a "high" or accelerated scenario.<ref>[https://aemo.com.au/-/media/files/electricity/wem/planning_and_forecasting/esoo/2023/2023-wholesale-electricity-market-electricity-statement-of-opportunities-wem-esoo.pdf?la=en 2023 Wholesale Electricity Market: Electricity Statement of Opportunities,] AEMO, August 2023</ref>

Despite AEMO's estimations and the plant's own financial stressors, Bluewaters Power still did not appear to have committed to a phase-out date as of 2024. In May 2024, the company's website stated the following regarding regarding the plant's future: "Based on our ongoing focus on continuously improving plant performance and the growing need for low-cost firming electricity supply, it is anticipated that Bluewaters Power will support the WA energy sector well into the future."<ref>[https://www.bluewatersps.com.au/our-future/#:~:text=Bluewaters%20Power%20is%20the%20newest,fired%20power%20stations%20by%202030. Our Future], Bluewaters Power, Accessed: May 13, 2024</ref> The company had not yet specified how far into the future the coal plant would continue to operate.

As of December 2024, the power station was reportedly expected to retire by 2031. Potential for an earlier retirement remained due to the lack of guaranteed coal supply from the Griffin coal mine beyond 2026.<ref>[https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2640109-western-australia-s-near-term-gas-supply-rises-aemo Western Australia's near-term gas supply rises: Aemo], Argus Media, December 19, 2024</ref>

In 2025, retirement plans for Bluewaters remained unclear. According to reporting from September 2025, AEMO estimated that Bluewaters would continue operating until at least 2028.<ref>[https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-09-18/wa-coal-phaseout-uncertain-amid-energy-grid-upgrade-plan/105788864 “WA coal phase-out uncertainty amid Bluewaters power station closure backflip,”] ABC News, September 17, 2025</ref> As of December 2025, public data from OpenElectricity indicated that Bluewaters was expected to close in 2030.<ref>[https://explore.openelectricity.org.au/facilities/wem/?selected=BLUEWATERS&tech=coal_black,coal_brown&status=operating “Bluewaters,”] OpenElectricity, accessed January 12, 2026</ref>

==Background on Bluewaters Power Station Expansion Project==

[[Griffin Energy]] proposed to add a further two 230 MW coal-fired generating units with a proposed commissioning date of 2012 and 2014 at the same location.<ref name=Hist>[http://www.bluewatersps.com.au/ourhistory.html "Our History"], Bluewaters Power website, accessed June 2014.</ref> The company stated that it "will also ensure the Bluewaters Power Station Expansion project will be capable of adopting [[Carbon Capture and Storage|carbon capture technology]] in the future, once this developing technology becomes commercially viable in Western Australia."<ref name=Prop>Griffin Energy, [http://www.griffinenergy.com.au/default.aspx?MenuID=310 "Bluewaters Power Station Expansion"], Griffin Energy, website, accessed August 2008.</ref>

Bluewaters Power states on its website that the two additional units would be 208 MW each and "are planned for completion in 2015" and that it "will be capable of adopting carbon capture technology in the future, once this developing technology becomes commercially viable in Western Australia."<ref>Bluewaters Power, [http://www.bluewatersps.com.au/bluewaterspowerstationexpansion.html "Bluewaters Power Station Expansion Project"], Bluewaters Power website, accessed June 2014.</ref>

However, the EPA were scathing in their 2010 assessment of the proposed plants carbon capture and storage element. While noting that the proposed plant would emit 3.1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions a year, the EPA wrote:<ref>Environmental Protection Agency, [http://www.epa.wa.gov.au/epadoclib/1349/Rep1349Blue3_4PER8310.pdf "Bluewaters Power Station Expansion - Phase III and Phase IV, Collie"], Environmental Protection Agency, March 2010, page 6.</ref>

:"Although the proponent intends to make sufficient space available on land immediately adjacent to each of the new generation plants to accommodate carbon capture related plant and equipment, it has not clearly indicated where this area of land is located within the proposed plant layout. Nor has the proponent confirmed that this area of land will be safeguarded against the construction of non-carbon capture related plant and equipment within it in the future."

:"The Lower Lesueur Formation and the Gage Sandstone geological formations have been identified by the proponent as potential geosequestration sites for the proposal. However, the proponent has not confirmed that these sites could accommodate the CO2 emissions from the Bluewaters Power Station Phase III and Phase IV generating plants over the anticipated life of the proposal. Considerable additional work needs to be undertaken to determine the viability of the Lower Lesueur Formation as a suitable geosequestration site. No detailed information was provided by the proponent in regard to the geosequestration potential of the Gage Sandstone formation. The proponent has not provided any information regarding the identification of potential transport routes to the above sites."

:"As a result, the EPA does not consider that the proponent has demonstrated that the project meets the IEA definition of CCS ready. Additionally, the likelihood that CCS will become technically and commercially viable is the near future is uncertain, and relying on CCS to constrain carbon emissions for this proposal in the future represents considerable risk."

In March 2015 the EPA issued a new review of the project and found that "the environmental factors of the proposal have not changed significantly" since the 2010 proposal, but recommended that the time limit of authorization of the expansion be extended by five years, to September 2020.<ref>[http://www.epa.wa.gov.au/EIA/EPAREPORTS/Pages/1543-BluewatersPowerStations46.aspx "Bluewaters Power Station Expansion - Phase III and Phase IV Proposal - inquiry under s46 of the Environmental Protection Act 1986 to amend Ministerial Statement 837,"] EPA, March 23, 2015</ref>

In December 2018, the owners of Bluewaters power station were reported to be looking for a $500 million dollar investment to replace existing facilities.<ref>Sarah Thompson and Anthony Macdonald, [https://www.afr.com/street-talk/wapower-producer-bluewaters-fronts-banks-for-new-loans-20181205-h18qv2 "WA-power producer Bluewaters fronts banks for new loans"] Financial Review, December 6, 2018</ref>

==Approval==

In March 2010 the Western Australian Environmental Protection Authority recommended to the Minister for the Environment that the Bluewaters Power Station Expansion Project be approved subject to a range conditions.<ref name=Recommend>Environmental Protection Authority, [http://www.epa.wa.gov.au/epadoclib/1349/Rep1349Blue3_4PER8310.pdf "Bluewaters Power Station Expansion - Phase III and Phase IV, Collie"], Environmental Protection Authority, March 2010.</ref>

In July 2010 the Western Australian Minister for the Environment, Donna Faragher, approved the expansion of the project subject to requiring the power station "to achieve continuous improvement in net greenhouse gas emissions through the adoption of advances in technology and process management. This includes consideration of carbon capture and storage and the use of new technologies to improve the efficiency of the generator units."<ref name=Go>Minister for the Environment, Donna Faragher, [https://www.wa.liberal.org.au/article/minister-determines-environmental-appeals-power-stations "Minister determines environmental appeals on power stations"], Media Release, July 11, 2010.</ref>

While the project has been approved, in June 2014 the Independent Market Operator - which assesses the adequacy of generation capacity to meet forecast electricity load -- stated that "no new capacity will be required in the SWIS until 2023-24" on its expected forecast.<ref name=IMO> Independent Market Operator, [http://www.imowa.com.au/docs/default-source/Reserve-Capacity/soo/imo_2014-swis-electricity-demand-outlook5EA7F337C272.pdf?sfvrsn=0 "SWIS Electricity Demand Outlook – June 2014"], Independent Market Operator, June 2014, page 3.</ref>

==Timeline==

* '''March 2010''': Western Australian Environmental Protection Authority recommends the Minister for the Environment approve the expansion subject to conditions;<ref name=Recommend>Environmental Protection Authority, [http://www.epa.wa.gov.au/epadoclib/1349/Rep1349Blue3_4PER8310.pdf "Bluewaters Power Station Expansion - Phase III and Phase IV, Collie"], Environmental Protection Authority, March 2010.</ref>

* '''July 2010''': Western Australian Minister for the Environment, Donna Faragher, approved the expansion;<ref name=Go>Minister for the Environment, Donna Faragher, [https://www.wa.liberal.org.au/article/minister-determines-environmental-appeals-power-stations "Minister determines environmental appeals on power stations"], Media Release, July 11, 2010.</ref>

* '''June 2014''': Independent Market Operator states that "no new capacity will be required in the SWIS until 2023-24" on its expected forecast.<ref name=IMO> Independent Market Operator, [http://www.imowa.com.au/docs/default-source/Reserve-Capacity/soo/imo_2014-swis-electricity-demand-outlook5EA7F337C272.pdf?sfvrsn=0 "SWIS Electricity Demand Outlook – June 2014"], Independent Market Operator, June 2014, page 3.</ref>

==Financing==

Financing for Kansai Electric Power and Sumitomo Corporation's acquisition of the power station in 2013 came in the form of A$922 million debt provided by a banking consortium comprising ANZ, Bank of Ireland, BayernLB, BBVA, BNP Paribas, Dexia Group, DZ Bank, GE Energy Financial Services, Intesa Sanpaolo, KBC Bank, NAB, OCBC Bank, Portigon, Societe Generale and Westpac<ref>[https://ijglobal.com/data/transaction/26556/acquisition-of-458mw-bluewaters-coal-fired-power-station-1-and-2 "Acquisition of 458MW Bluewaters Coal-fired Power station 1 and 2"], IJGlobal, accessed Jul. 2020</ref>

The project would be built under a BOT (build, operate, transfer) arrangement by Korean Electric Power Corporation and Vinakobalt Long An.<Ref>[http://www.talkvietnam.com/2015/10/major-coal-fired-power-plant-near-ho-chi-minh-city-likely/ "Major coal-fired power plant near Ho Chi Minh City likely,"] Thanhiennews, October 9, 2015</ref> As of November 2019 there has been no progress in over years, including no mention in Vietnam's long-range planning documents, and it appears that the project is cancelled.

==Financing==

*'''Source of financing:''' '''US$33.9 million''' government guarantee from the World Bank; '''US$3.4 billion''' in debt from Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), MUFG Bank, Mizuho Financial Group, Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking, Norinchukin Bank, Shinsei Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Holdings, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, DBS Bank and Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation; '''US$879 million''' in equity from Adaro Energy, Itochu and J-Power

==Background==

In October 2011, two Japanese companies (utility [[J-POWER]] and [[Itochu]], a conglomerate with major coal interests) teamed up with Indonesia-based [[Adaro Power]] (a subsidiary of [[Adaro Energy]]) to build a large coal-fired power plant using advanced [[ultra-supercritical]] technology. The three companies formed [[PT Bhimasena Power Indonesia]] to operate the plant, with power being sold to [[PT Perusahaan Listrik Negara]] (PT PLN), Indonesia's state-owned utility. Originally, the plan was for the first 1,000 MW unit to begin operating in late 2016, followed by the second 1,000 MW unit in 2017. If built, it will be the largest coal plant in Indonesia.<ref name="Bloomberg">Emi Urabe, Tsuyoshi Inajima and Fitri Wulandari, [http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-10-04/j-power-partners-delay-4-billion-indonesia-coal-power-plant.html "J-Power, Partners Delay $4 Billion Indonesia Coal Power Plant,"] Bloomberg News, October 3, 2013</ref>

The project was initially planned for commissioning by 2016, but has faced opposition from landowners and environmental groups,<ref name="nar">[http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Business-Briefs/Adaro-venture-backs-out-of-Central-Java-power-project "Adaro venture backs out of Central Java power project,"] Nikei Asian Review, July 8, 2014.</ref> and delays in acquiring land and completing environmental assessments.<ref name="Bloomberg">Emi Urabe, Tsuyoshi Inajima and Fitri Wulandari, [http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-10-04/j-power-partners-delay-4-billion-indonesia-coal-power-plant.html "J-Power, Partners Delay $4 Billion Indonesia Coal Power Plant,"] Bloomberg News, October 3, 2013</ref> To override local opposition, the government invoked the 2012 Land Acquisition Law, which enables land procurement in the name of the public interest. In April 2015 the government said it would start the construction on the plant at the end of the month, despite protests by local people.<ref name="rc">Raras Cahyafitri, [http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2015/04/08/construction-batang-power-plant-start-end-month.html#sthash.F8DV7N1k.dpuf "Construction of Batang power plant to start end of this month,"] The Jakarta Post, April 08 2015</ref> Unit 1 is now planned for commissioning in 2018, and Unit 2 in 2019.<ref name="LT">[http://energy-indonesia.com/03dge/0140317pln.pdf “PLN Long Term Electricity Plan (2013-2023),”] presentation by Moch. Sofyan, Head of New & Renewable Division of PT PLN (Persero), 06 March 2014</ref> 

On April 30, 2015, Masayoshi Kitamura, president of J-Power, said, "We will start construction as soon as possible, at least by Oct. 6."<ref>Fitri Wulandari and Emi Urabe, [http://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-05-04/how-not-to-build-a-power-plant-a-tale-from-java-island "How not to build a power plant: a tale from Java Island,"] Bloomberg Business, 4 May 2015</ref> On August 28, 2015, President Joko Widodo performed a ground-breaking ceremony at the plant site.<ref>[http://en.tempo.co/read/news/2015/08/26/056695170/Batang-Steam-Power-Plant-to-Kick-off-Friday "Batang Steam Power Plant to Kick off Friday,"] Tempo, 26 August 2015</ref> Activists denounced the ceremony as a publicity stunt, pointing out that in reality landowners continued to refuse to sell about 10 percent of the 226 hectares needed by the project.<ref>Arif Fiyanto, [http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2015/09/04/jokowi-s-misleading-view-batang-plant.html "Jokowi’s misleading view of Batang plant,"] Jakarta Post, 4 September 2015</ref>

In late September 2015, J-Power said it would miss the Oct. 6 deadline to provide initial funding for the plant due to long-running land disputes.<ref>[http://af.reuters.com/article/energyOilNews/idAFL3N11Y10W20150928?pageNumber=1&virtualBrandChannel=0 "Indonesia to miss funding deadline for $4 bln power plant,"] Reuters, Sep 28, 2015</ref>

In February 2016, the Supreme Court rejected a challenge by residents against lower court approval of the siting of the plant in central Java. The community is considering other legal options. The first unit is now planned for 2020.<ref name="fs">Fedina S. Sundaryani, [http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2016/03/02/supreme-court-ruling-paves-way-batang-megaproject.html#sthash.XEnL4n0R.p72mofxa.dpuf "Supreme Court ruling paves way for Batang megaproject,"] The Jakarta Post, March 02 2016</ref> In March 2016, it was reported the plant was beginning the construction phase.<ref>[http://www.rambuenergy.com/2016/03/giant-power-plant-pltu-batang-enters-construction-phase/ "Giant power plant PLTU Batang enters construction phase,"] Rambu Energy, March 25, 2016</ref> In June 2016, JBIC approved a US$3.4 billion loan agreement for the plant.<ref>[http://www.banktrack.org/show/news/banktrack_condemns_japanese_and_singapore_bank_financing_of_batang_coal_project_in_indonesia_as_reckless_to_people_and_climate "BankTrack condemns Japanese and Singapore bank financing of Batang coal project in Indonesia as reckless to people and climate,"] Banktrack, June 6, 2016</ref> The project would consist of two 950 MW units.<ref name="LTP">[http://www.djk.esdm.go.id/pdf/RUPTL/RUPTL%20PLN%202016-2025.pdf “Rencana Usaha Penyediaan Tenaga Listrik, PT PLN (Persero), 2016-2025,”] Kementerian Energi Dan Sumber Daya Mineral, June 2016</ref>

In March 2018, PT Bhimasena stated that construction was 40% complete.<ref>[http://industri.bisnis.com/read/20180318/44/751181/pltu-batang-ditargetkan-mulai-beroperasi-penuh-pada-2020 PLTU Batang Ditargetkan Mulai Beroperasi Penuh Pada 2020], Industri, Mar. 18, 2018</ref>

In February 2019, the government's long-range plan for 2019-2028 listed the project with a completion date of 2020.<ref name="RUPTL2019">[http://listrik.org/pln/ruptl/ Rencana Usaha Penyediaan Tenaga Listrik (RUPTL) 2019-2028,] PT PLN Persero, V-43</ref> In October 2019, construction was reportedly 83% complete and the plant was expected to be commissioned in 2020.<ref name="tjp1">[https://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2019/10/04/indonesia-s-largest-power-plant-schedule-operate-next-year.html Indonesia’s largest power plant on schedule to operate next year], The Jakarta Post, Oct. 4, 2019</ref> In April 2020, a House of Representatives faction of the Bataang regency recommended to the national government that construction of the plant be temporarily halted due to the Covid-19 pandemic.<ref>[https://ekonomi.bisnis.com/read/20200414/44/1226763/dprd-batang-usul-proyek-pltu-disetop-sementara-ini-kata-bupati DPRD Batang Usul Proyek PLTU Disetop Sementara, Ini Kata Bupati], Ekonomi, Apr. 14, 2020</ref> Construction was 93.6% complete as of Q1 2020.<ref>[https://market.bisnis.com/read/20200708/192/1263394/di-balik-riuhnya-kawasan-industri-batang-adaro-adro-pacu-penyelesaian-pltu-bpi Di Balik Riuhnya Kawasan Industri Batang, Adaro (ADRO) Pacu Penyelesaian PLTU BPI], Bisnis, Jul. 8, 2020</ref>

In October 2020, Adaro announced a target start date of the end of 2021.<ref name=cnbc2020>[https://www.cnbcindonesia.com/market/20201020171701-17-195804/tertunda-adaro-targetkan-pltu-batang-beroperasi-akhir-2021 Tertunda, Adaro Targetkan PLTU Batang Beroperasi Akhir 2021], CNBC Indonesia, Oct. 20, 2020</ref> In April 2021, it was reported that construction was more than 94% complete.<ref name=bisnis>[https://market.bisnis.com/read/20210420/192/1383712/adaro-adro-targetkan-pltu-batang-rampung-awal-2022 Adaro Targets PLTU Batang Completion in Early 2022], Bisnis, Apr. 20, 2021</ref>

In August 2022, the power station appeared to be in the testing phase for commercial operation or COD. Both units were reportedly 97.7% complete.<ref>[https://market.bisnis.com/read/20220802/192/1561854/adaro-adro-persiapkan-cod-pltu-batang-2x11000-mw-tambah-cuan Adaro ADRO Persiapkan COD PLTU Batang 2x1.1000 MW, Tambah Cuan], Bisnis, Aug. 2, 2022</ref>

In an October 2022 weekly newsletter, the power station was mentioned as officially operational since August 31, 2022.<ref name =kpbu>[https://kpbu.kemenkeu.go.id/read/1100-1263/umum/newsletter-kantor-bersama-kpbu PPP Joint Office Newsletter: 145th Edition], Kerjasama Pemerintah dan Badan Usaha, October 2022</ref>

In early 2023, the power station was listed as a 2022 achievement.<ref>phttps://voi.id/ekonomi/249884/progres-proyek-listrik-35-gw-baru-47-persen-hingga-desember-2022 "Progres Proyek Listrik 35 GW Baru 47 Persen hingga Desember 2022,"] VOI, Feb. 1, 2023</ref>

In November 2024, the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources designated Central Java Power Project as a Objek Vital Nasional (national vital object).<ref>[https://www.suara.com/bisnis/2024/11/07/131833/pltu-batang-jadi-pilar-strategis-energi-nasional-dan-pendorong-perekonomian-daerah "PLTU Batang Jadi Pilar Strategis Energi Nasional dan Pendorong Perekonomian Daerah,"] Suara.com, November 7, 2024</ref>

==Funding==

===World Bank Support===
The [[World Bank and coal|World Bank's]] Indonesia Infrastructure Guarantee Fund (IIGF) awarded its first government guarantee of US$33.9 million to the project. The bank also served as the transaction advisor for the project, arranging financing and promoting the project to investors.<ref name="Price">[http://priceofoil.org/content/uploads/2013/09/OCI_World_Bank_Indonesia_Coal_09_2013.pdf "World Bank Accelerating Coal Development in Indonesia,"] Oil Change International, September 2013</ref>
====Critics accuse World Bank of using "back door means" to skirt restrictions and avoid transparency====
All of the World Bank Group’s activities surrounding the Central Java Power Project add up to as much or more involvement than is typically expended for a direct project investment by the World Bank Group. However, because the World Bank Group has approached this project through back door means, i.e., financial intermediaries and off-budget grants for technical assistance, this mega coal project did not have to meet the World Bank Group’s criteria for coal lending, including full consideration of alternatives, internalizing the cost of carbon, and optimizing energy efficiency and conservation measures. Such an approach has also resulted in less international scrutiny and transparency than is typically involved in Bank-supported coal developments.<ref name="Price">[http://priceofoil.org/content/uploads/2013/09/OCI_World_Bank_Indonesia_Coal_09_2013.pdf "World Bank Accelerating Coal Development in Indonesia,"] Oil Change International, September 2013</ref>
===JBIC===
In August 2014 it was reported that the Japanese Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) was considering funding 60% (over 400 billion yen) of the plant’s construction, using public funds.<ref>[http://sekitan.jp/jbic/?p=648&lang=en "Standing up against Japan’s coal-fired power plant export: Locals affected by the Batang coal-fired power plant project speak out,"] No Coal, Go Green, August 19, 2014.</ref>

In June 2016, JBIC approved a US$3.4 billion loan agreement for the 2,000 MW project, joined by a string of commercial banks: Japanese banks MUFG Bank, Mizuho Financial Group, Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking, Norinchukin Bank, Shinsei Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Holdings, and Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, and two Singapore based banks, DBS Bank and Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation.<ref>[http://www.banktrack.org/show/news/banktrack_condemns_japanese_and_singapore_bank_financing_of_batang_coal_project_in_indonesia_as_reckless_to_people_and_climate "BankTrack condemns Japanese and Singapore bank financing of Batang coal project in Indonesia as reckless to people and climate,"] Banktrack, June 6, 2016</ref><ref name="IJGlobal"> [https://ijglobal.com/data/transaction/19236/central-java-coal-fired-power-plant-2000mw-ppp "Central Java Coal-Fired Power Plant (2000MW) PPP"], IJGlobal, accessed Sep. 16, 2020</ref> 

===Equity===
Adaro Energy, Itochu and J-Power provided US$879 million in equity for the project.<ref name="IJGlobal"> [https://ijglobal.com/data/transaction/19236/central-java-coal-fired-power-plant-2000mw-ppp "Central Java Coal-Fired Power Plant (2000MW) PPP"], IJGlobal, accessed Sep. 16, 2020</ref>

==Environmental Impacts==

According to Greenpeace Indonesia, the planned site for the plant is in the Ujungnegoro-Roban coastal area, which is a marine conservation area and was declared an area for development of marine tourism under Government Regulation No. 26/2008. The plant will infringe upon a protected area, in direct contravention of Central Java provincial bylaw No 6/2010 on spatial planning. If construction of this coal plant goes ahead at least five villages in the Batang area will be demolished, and hundreds of hectares of jasmine, plantations and paddy fields will be destroyed. Arif Fiyanto of Greenpeace Indonesia said, “The planned coal plant will pollute rich coastal fishing waters and threaten the livelihoods of more than 10,000 small-scale fishermen.” Greenpeace also reported that the plant will emit 226 kg of mercury per year.<ref>Siaran Pers, [http://www.greenpeace.org/seasia/id/press/releases/Batang-Coal-fired-Power-Plant-Will-destroy-health-and-livelihoods/ "Batang coal-fired power plant will destroy health and livelihoods,"] Greenpeace Indonesia, April 3, 2013</ref>

In July 2025, Indonesia’s Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries granted permission for the Central Java Power Project to use seawater for cooling, raising concerns from marine experts on the impact of heated discharge on coastal ecosystems and fisheries. The power station reportedly used approximately 3 billion cubic meters of seawater each year. The People’s Coalition for Fisheries Justice (KIARA) called for an environmental impact assessment “to ensure that the seawater intake and discharge of heated water from the power plant’s operations do not pollute or damage the surrounding marine ecosystem and do not harm the livelihoods of traditional fishers in the area.”<ref>[https://news.mongabay.com/2025/07/batang-coal-plants-seawater-permit-imperils-marine-life-fishing-communities/ “Batang coal plant’s seawater permit imperils marine life, fishing communities,”] Mongabay, July 26, 2025</ref>

==Opposition==

Around 7,000 residents of the five villages affected by the project are strongly opposed to its construction. In addition, a range of environmental and human rights groups have protested the project.<ref>Kate Sheppard, [http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/09/25/world-bank-coal_n_3986125.html "World Bank Aids New Coal Project Abroad, Defying Policy, Environmental Group Says,"] Huffington Post, September 25, 2013</ref> About 74 farmers from four villages in Central Java’s Batang regency have refused to sell their land for the project.<ref>[http://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-05-04/how-not-to-build-a-power-plant-a-tale-from-java-island "How Not to Build a Power Plant: a Tale From Java Island,"] Bloomberg, May 4, 2015</ref> 

===December 2015: National Human Rights Commission===
In December 2015, the National Human Rights Commission, an Indonesian state-sanctioned but independent group, sent letters to Prime Minister Abe and the Japanese parliament requesting that greater attention be paid to human rights issues associated with the plant. The letter stated that since 2013, a pressure campaign had been conducted against hold-out landowners “including intimidations and physical and mental threats.” According to additional comments by commissioner Dianto Bachriadi, heavy machines driven by military soldiers hired by the government and the consortium made canals surrounding the properties of local people who were refusing to sell. “It has made them isolated. People from outside can’t go in and the residents can’t bring their products out,” he said. According to Bachriadi, the commission had previously recommended that the project site be moved to a less-populated and less-conflicted area, but the recommendation was ignored.<ref>[http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/01/09/national/indonesian-rights-commission-tells-japan-review-power-project/#.VyvkwBUrKem "Indonesian rights commission tells Japan to review power project,"] Japan Times, January 9, 2016</ref>

===July 2015: JBIC protest===
In July 2015, three villagers affected by the proposed plant traveled to Tokyo to personally deliver an official objection to the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), the public financial institution considering funding the project. The objection filed with JBIC was signed by 23 leaders of the local community organization known as Paguyuban UKPWR. The communities also filed a complaint against Japanese companies Itochu and J-Power under the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. The communities allege that JBIC has violated its social and environmental guidelines in proceeding with the project.<ref>[http://endcoal.org/2015/08/in-japan-indonesian-villagers-file-official-complaints-on-batang-coal-plant/ "In Japan, Indonesian Villagers File Official Complaints on Batang Coal Plant,"] EndCoal, August 12, 2015</ref> 

===Protest at Japanese embassy (July 22, 2013)===
[[File:July 22-2013-Jakarta-protest.jpg|thumb|right|upright=2|"Reject Batang Power Plant," July 22, 2013 protest at Japanese embassy in Jakarta. Photo courtesy of GreenpeaceIndonesia]]
On July 22, 2013, about 150 people protested against the project in front of the Japanese Embassy in Jakarta. The protesters were members of Paguyuban Rakyat Batang Berjuang Untuk Konservasi, supported by Yayasan Lembaga Bantuan Hukum Indonesia (YLBHI), or Indonesia Legal Aid Foundation (YLBHI). According to protesters, the project would heavily impact the livelihoods of thousands of fishermen due to its effects on coral reefs and other environmentally sensitive areas. In addition, the 200-500 acres used by the project would destroy irrigated rice fields and tens of thousands of trees. Among the protesters was M. Ali Tafrihan of Roban village, who reported being jailed for six months as a result of his opposition to the project.<ref>Siaran Pers, [http://www.greenpeace.org/seasia/id/press/releases/stop-investasi-jahat-jepang-di-pltu-batang/ "Stop Investasi Jahat Jepang di PLTU Batang,"] Greenpeace Indonesia press release, July 22, 2013</ref>

===Human Rights Violations===
According to Lembaga Bantuan Hukum (LBH) Semarang, a legal aid organization that has been working with residents at the project site, thugs as well as police and members of the military have used intimidation tactics against those who have refused to sell their land.<ref name="Monga">Diana Parker, [http://news.mongabay.com/2013/0326-parker-coal-plant-java.html "Indonesia's largest coal plant will be built despite protests, minister says,"] Mongabay.com, May 26, 2013</ref>

===Other Opposition===

From 2011-2014, over 7,000 villagers near the Batang power plant staged more than 22 protests against the construction of Southeast Asia’s largest coal-fired power plant. Citing how the World Bank and Japan are helping fund the Batang power plant, Greenpeace joined the Batang communities and created a report in opposition to “investing in dirty fossil fuels.”<ref>[https://www.banktrack.org/download/the_true_cost_of_coal/the_true_cost_of_coal_greenpeace.pdf/ "The True Cost of Coal,"] ''Greenpeace'', Mar. 2014</ref>

On May 6, 2014, local residents of Batang, Central Java province in Indonesia protested against the Batang power plant in front of the Batang State Attorney Office. The protests resulted in a violent class with local police. Protestors believe that the power plant would have negative impacts on the community near Batang.<ref>[https://sekitan.jp/jbic/en/2014/05/12/578/ "Human Rights Violations Continue, Residents Attacked Again in Violent Clash with Police,"] ''Stop Japanese Coal Finance'', 12 May. 2014</ref>

On May 1, 2015, a petition started to call the Indonesian president, Jokowi Widodo, to stop the construction of the Batang coal power plant. Citing how local villagers near Batang and rice farmers have refused to cooperate with the coal plant project, the petition demands that the Indonesian government stop “this dirty project.” The project is believed to eventually harm rice fields, destroy fisheries, and emit toxic air pollution.<ref>[https://secure.avaaz.org/community_petitions/en/Indonesian_President_Joko_Widodo_Stop_the_Central_Java_Coal_Plant/?nkHCqjb/ "Stop the Central Java Coal Plant!"] ''Avaaz.org'', 1 May. 2015</ref>

In May 2016, about 3,500 people staged a protest in the capital of Indonesia against the development of the Batang power plant. Organized by environmental groups, the protest started from the Japanese Embassy to the presidential palace.<ref>[https://ejatlas.org/conflict/batang-coal-mining-central-java-indonesia/ "Batang coal fired power plant, Central Java, Indonesia,"] ''Environmental Justice Atlas'', 21 Sep. 2017</ref>

On March 30, 2017, activists stopped construction at the Batang power plant for 13 hours. Activists demand for the Indonesian government and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) to pull their financial support of the coal plant. The protestors are motivated by how the Batang plant would “contribute to 6500 premature deaths in Nindonesia every year linked to air pollution from burning coal.” Furthermore, local fishermen joined the activists’ blockade because the coal plant has made it harder to catch fish.<ref>[https://dominicantoday.com/dr/world/2017/03/30/activists-stop-construction-at-southeast-asias-biggest-planned-coal-plant/ "Activists stop construction at Southeast Asia's biggest planned coal plant,"] ''Dominican Today'', 30 Mar. 2017</ref> Activists from Greenpeace, Indonesian Forum for Environment (WALHI) and Mining Advocacy Network (JATAM) also joined the blockade of the coal plant.<ref>[https://jakartaglobe.id/multimedia/protests-coal-fired-power-plant-central-java/ "Protests Against Coal-Fired Power Plant in Central Java,"] ''Jakarta Globe'', 31 Mar. 2017</ref>

In January 2023, former landowners continued to protest at the entrance of the power station. According to organizers, residents were underpaid for their land in 2012, and they would continue actions under their demands were met.<ref>[https://jateng.inews.id/berita/ratusan-warga-demo-di-pintu-masuk-pltu-batang-ini-tuntutannya "Ratusan Warga Demo di Pintu Masuk PLTU Batang, Ini Tuntutannya,"] ''iNews Jateng'', January 17, 2023</ref>

==Delays==

In July 2013 Bloomberg reported that the plant was delayed due to difficulties acquiring land, environmental assessments, and local opposition. As a result of the problems, the onset of construction was reportedly postposed by two years, from October 2012 to October 2014.<ref name="Bloomberg">Emi Urabe, Tsuyoshi Inajima and Fitri Wulandari, [http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-10-04/j-power-partners-delay-4-billion-indonesia-coal-power-plant.html "J-Power, Partners Delay $4 Billion Indonesia Coal Power Plant,"] Bloomberg News, October 3, 2013</ref> According to a spokesman for J-POWER, 80 percent of land needed for the project had been acquired.<ref name="Bloomberg">Emi Urabe, Tsuyoshi Inajima and Fitri Wulandari, [http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-10-04/j-power-partners-delay-4-billion-indonesia-coal-power-plant.html "J-Power, Partners Delay $4 Billion Indonesia Coal Power Plant,"] Bloomberg News, October 3, 2013</ref>

===Local landowners could derail project===
[[File:Central_Java_protest.jpg|thumb|right|upright=2|Protest against Central Java Power Project, (undated) Photo courtesy of GreenpeaceIndonesia]]
{{#ev:youtube|WyEkfzBjEi4|600|right|Residents speak out against Central Java Project, November 25, 2013. Courtesy of GreenpeaceIndonesia.}}
According to a July 2013 story in the Japan Times, around 50 landowners at the project site were refusing to sell 40 hectares, an amount of land amounting to 20 percent of the land needed to build the project. If the land purchase was not completed by October 6, the sponsors of the project would lose the right to build the project and a new round of bidding would need to be conducted. According to an unnamed Indonesian official, completing the acquisition by the October deadline would be virtually impossible.<ref name="Times">[http://bit.ly/KhJY1k "Locals stall $4 billion Indonesia power plant,"] Japan Times, July 20, 2013</ref> According to a report in the environmental blog Mongabay, opponents of the plant were disputing government claims regarding the amount of land that had been secured. Roidhi, a resident of Karanggenang, one of the villages affected by the project, told Mongabay that "70 percent of our land still belongs to us." "When you look at the data mentioned by Hatta Rajasa...and Lucy Eko Wuryanto it is very clear that the data mentioned is a mere claim. Each person is reporting different data," said Wahyu Nandang Herawan, a staff member of Lembaga Bantuan Hukum (LBH) Semarang, a legal aid organization that has been working with the community. <ref name="Monga">Diana Parker, [http://news.mongabay.com/2013/0326-parker-coal-plant-java.html "Indonesia's largest coal plant will be built despite protests, minister says,"] Mongabay.com, May 26, 2013</ref>

===Project wins one-year extension===
In October 2013, a decree by President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono revised a regulation that required the project one year after signing its contract to secure financial backing. Following the extension, the Jakarta Post reported that the consortium sponsoring the project and the government "are working on a persuasive approach to win the hearts of local residents." Garibaldi Thohir, president of Adaro Energy, said, "The important thing now is how to approach the community. I myself, along with Pak Ganjar will take part in the socialization program." Ganjar Pranowo is the governor of Centra Java.<ref>[http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2013/11/04/consortium-use-new-approach-stalled-plant.html "Consortium to use new approach in stalled plant,"] Jakarta Post, November 4, 2013</ref>

===BPI declares force majeure===
In June 2014 PT Adaro said Bhimasena Power Indonesia (BPI), the project's joint venture between Japan's J-Power, Itochu, and Adaro subsidiary Adaro Power, declared force majeure with suppliers and Indonesia state-owned electricity company PLN on June 27, 2014, due to delays in acquiring the necessary land. Force majeure is a legal clause that allows companies to walk away from contracts soured by external events.<ref name="nar">[http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Business-Briefs/Adaro-venture-backs-out-of-Central-Java-power-project "Adaro venture backs out of Central Java power project,"] Nikei Asian Review, July 8, 2014.</ref> 

In a statement, BPI said the consortium had acquired more than 85 percent of the land needed for the project as well as approval for its environmental impact assessment and other necessary permits but, "due to the instability of the situation at the site, the acquisition of the remaining plots of land are beyond the reasonable ability of a private company, like BPI, to acquire and may be acquired only with government support.”<ref name="nar">[http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Business-Briefs/Adaro-venture-backs-out-of-Central-Java-power-project "Adaro venture backs out of Central Java power project,"] Nikei Asian Review, July 8, 2014.</ref>

BPI is committed to continue the project, the statement said.<ref name="nar">[http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Business-Briefs/Adaro-venture-backs-out-of-Central-Java-power-project "Adaro venture backs out of Central Java power project,"] Nikei Asian Review, July 8, 2014.</ref>

==Cost Escalation==

Originally the project was estimated to cost US$3.2 billion. In October 2013, Boy Garibaldi Thohir, president director of Adaro Energy, said that the cost of the project had risen significantly. Boy declined to state an exact figure but said that the total was not more than $5 billion. The cost increases have delayed the financial closing of the project.<ref>Retno Ayuningtyas, [http://www.thejakartaglobe.com/business/investment-for-central-java-power-plant-to-soar/ "Investment for Central Java Power Plant to Soar,"] Jakarta Globe, October 17, 2013</ref>

In 2015 the cost was estimated at US$4 billion.<ref name="rc">Raras Cahyafitri, [http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2015/04/08/construction-batang-power-plant-start-end-month.html#sthash.F8DV7N1k.dpuf "Construction of Batang power plant to start end of this month,"] The Jakarta Post, April 08 2015</ref>

==High Efficiency Technology and Japan's International Economic Strategy==

The project will use [[ultra-supercritical]] technology, which offers combustion efficiency of 43 percent. The relative reduction in carbon dioxide emissions provided by the high efficiency of the combustion technology has been cited by Japan's prime minister Shinzo Abe, among others, as an argument for constructing the plant.<ref>[http://www.kantei.go.jp/foreign/96_abe/statement/201310/07koen_e.html "Keynote Address by Prime Minister Shinzo Abe at the APEC CEO Summit 2013,"] Prime Minister of Japan and His Cabinet website, October 7, 2013</ref> According to the Nikkei Asian Review, promoting of ultra-supercritical technology as a climate change solution is linked to Japanese government efforts to assist Japanese businesses against Chinese rivals for coveted overseas power plant construction contracts. "We want to make the Central Java project a showcase that will open the door to more projects," said an official at Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry.<ref>Hirofumi Matsuo, [http://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Trends/Prospects-dimming-for-key-Japanese-power-plant-in-Indonesia "Prospects dimming for key Japanese power plant in Indonesia,"] Nikkei Asian Review, November 28, 2013</ref>

==Timeline==

*October 2011 - joint venture formed
*October 2012 - original plan for beginning of construction
*October 2013 - companies announce that construction would be delayed at least two years due to environmental assessments, local opposition, and difficulties acquiring land.
*April 2014 - Coordinating Economic Minister Hatta Rajasa says 29 ha of land are still in question from the 226 ha needed for the megaproject.
*June 2014 - Bhimasena Power Indonesia declares force majeure, a legal clause that allows companies to walk away from contracts soured by external events.
*Mar 2015 - Batang residents and Greenpeace Indonesia activists protest a statement made by President Jokowi in which he claimed that obstacles hampering the construction of the plant had been overcome.<ref name="fs">Fedina S. Sundaryani, [http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2016/03/02/supreme-court-ruling-paves-way-batang-megaproject.html#sthash.XEnL4n0R.p72mofxa.dpuf "Supreme Court ruling paves way for Batang megaproject,"] The Jakarta Post, March 02 2016</ref>
*Aug. 28, 2015 - Jokowi officiates the ground-breaking ceremony for the project, although 11.1 ha of land still needed.<ref name="fs">Fedina S. Sundaryani, [http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2016/03/02/supreme-court-ruling-paves-way-batang-megaproject.html#sthash.XEnL4n0R.p72mofxa.dpuf "Supreme Court ruling paves way for Batang megaproject,"] The Jakarta Post, March 02 2016</ref>
*April 2017 - Construction described as "30 percent from completion" by PT Adaro Energy president Garibaldi Thohir<ref>[https://www.rambuenergy.com/2017/04/adaro-mega-power-plant-pltu-batang-making-good-progress/ "Adaro: mega power plant PLTU Batang making good progress,"] RambuEnergy, 27 April 2017</ref>
*September 2018 - Construction described as 50 percent complete, with a target date of 2020 for commissioning.<ref>[https://industri.kontan.co.id/news/adaro-energy-adro-pastikan-proyek-pltu-bakal-rampung-tepat-waktu Adaro Energy (ADRO) pastikan proyek PLTU bakal rampung tepat waktu], Kontan, Sep. 23, 2018</ref>
*December 2018 - Construction described as 63 percent complete.<ref>[http://akurat.co/ekonomi/id-420273-read-rini-dorong-perkembangan-industri-di-batang-pasca-pembangunan-pltu Rini Dorong Perkembangan Industri di Batang Pasca Pembangunan PLTU], Akurat, Dec. 5, 2018</ref>
*October 2019 - Construction described as 83 percent complete.<ref name="tjp1">[https://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2019/10/04/indonesia-s-largest-power-plant-schedule-operate-next-year.html Indonesia’s largest power plant on schedule to operate next year], The Jakarta Post, Oct. 4, 2019</ref>
*April 2021 - Construction described as 94 percent complete.<ref name=bisnis>[https://market.bisnis.com/read/20210420/192/1383712/adaro-adro-targetkan-pltu-batang-rampung-awal-2022 Adaro Targets PLTU Batang Completion in Early 2022], Bisnis, Apr. 20, 2021</ref>
*August 2022 - The power station was operational.<ref name =kpbu>[https://kpbu.kemenkeu.go.id/read/1100-1263/umum/newsletter-kantor-bersama-kpbu PPP Joint Office Newsletter: 145th Edition], Kerjasama Pemerintah dan Badan Usaha, October 2022</ref>
